title: Microsoft Fundamentals
tagline: AZ-900 / AI-900 / DP-900 / SC-900 in one sweep
disclaimer: Independent practice material by Interstitium Labs. Not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Microsoft. Confers no certificate. All scenarios are original; no exam content is reproduced.

scenarios.title: The server room invoice
scenarios.situation: A small firm's finance lead complains that every server refresh means a painful capital outlay, and half the racks sit idle between projects.
scenarios.prompt: Which cloud characteristic directly solves this spending pattern?
choices: Pay-as-you-go pricing converts capital expense into operational expense
Regions let you pick where data lives
Resource groups enforce naming standards
Availability zones add redundancy
scenarios.why: Cloud's consumption model shifts IT spend from CapEx (upfront hardware purchases) to OpEx (pay only for what you use), which is exactly why idle on-premises capacity is wasteful. You scale resources up and down and the bill follows actual usage.
scenarios.hint: Think about when the money is spent: before you use anything, or as you use it?

scenarios.title: The hospital's hybrid call
scenarios.situation: A regional hospital wants patient records in its own datacenter for regulatory reasons but wants burst capacity for its public appointment portal.
choices: Public cloud only
Private cloud only
Hybrid cloud
Multi-cloud with no on-premises footprint
scenarios.why: Hybrid cloud combines on-premises/private infrastructure with public cloud, keeping sensitive workloads local while bursting to the cloud. Multi-cloud means multiple public providers, which is a different concept.
scenarios.hint: They want to keep one foot in their own datacenter — what model has a foot in both worlds?

scenarios.title: Black Friday traffic
scenarios.situation: An e-commerce site sees 10x traffic for six hours on Black Friday, then returns to normal. Last year the site crashed.
scenarios.prompt: Which capability should the architect rely on?
choices: Elasticity — automatically add and remove capacity as demand changes
Scalability — permanently buying bigger servers once
High availability — running in two regions always
Fault tolerance — duplicating every database write
scenarios.why: Elasticity is the ability to automatically scale out and back in as demand fluctuates — perfect for short spikes. Scalability is the capacity to handle growth, but elasticity specifically covers the automatic, temporary dimension.
scenarios.hint: The key word is 'then returns to normal' — which capability goes both directions automatically?

scenarios.title: The deleted project
scenarios.situation: A team deletes a resource group called 'pilot-web' and is surprised when the app service, database, and storage account inside it all disappear.
scenarios.prompt: What is the fundamental rule they missed?
evidence: DELETE resource group pilot-web — initiated by admin@contoso.com
app-pilot (App Service), sqldb-pilot (SQL Database), stpilotdata (Storage) → all in pilot-web
choices: Resources inherit the lifecycle of their resource group — deleting the group deletes everything in it
Resource groups can only hold one resource type
Deleting a group moves resources to a recycle bin for 90 days
Resource groups are just billing labels with no real effect
scenarios.why: A resource group is a lifecycle and management boundary: delete it and every resource inside is deleted too. That's why teams organize groups by project or environment — so cleanup is one deliberate action, not an accident.
scenarios.hint: What happened to the children when the parent container was removed?

scenarios.title: One datacenter goes dark
scenarios.situation: A company runs its VMs in a single datacenter within East US. A power event takes that datacenter offline and the app goes down.
scenarios.prompt: What design would have kept the app running?
choices: Deploying across availability zones — separate datacenters within the same region
Picking a region closer to users
Adding a second resource group
Enabling a longer backup retention policy
scenarios.why: Availability zones are physically separate datacenters within one Azure region with independent power, cooling, and networking. Spreading VMs across zones survives a single-datacenter failure; a second region would also work but zones are the in-region answer.
scenarios.hint: The failure was one building. What Azure construct is literally 'separate buildings in the same region'?

scenarios.title: Patch Tuesday outage
scenarios.situation: An admin deploys twelve VMs into an availability set. During host patching, several VMs reboot at the same time and the app stutters.
choices: Update domains — VMs should be spread across them so planned maintenance reboots only one group at a time
Fault domains — they protect against patching, not hardware failure
Resource locks — they would have blocked the patching
Proximity placement groups — they guarantee patching order
scenarios.why: Update domains group VMs that can be rebooted together during planned host maintenance; spreading VMs across update domains keeps some running while others patch. Fault domains protect against unplanned hardware failure — a different axis.
scenarios.hint: Patching is planned maintenance. Which domain type exists for planned events?

scenarios.title: Labeling the project
scenarios.situation: A manager calls their new churn-prediction model 'an AI' in one slide, 'machine learning' in the next, and 'deep learning' in the next. The team is confused.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct relationship between the three terms?
choices: AI is the broad field; machine learning is a subset of AI; deep learning is a subset of machine learning
Deep learning is the broad field containing AI and machine learning
The three terms are interchangeable synonyms
Machine learning contains AI, which contains deep learning
scenarios.why: Artificial intelligence is the umbrella (any machine performing human-like tasks). Machine learning is the AI subset where systems learn from data instead of explicit rules. Deep learning is the ML subset using multi-layer neural networks.
scenarios.hint: Think of nested boxes — which box is the biggest?
objectives: AI vs ML vs deep learning

scenarios.title: Predicting house prices
scenarios.situation: A team has a spreadsheet of 10,000 past home sales with sale prices, and wants to predict the price of new listings.
choices: Supervised learning — regression on labeled historical prices
Unsupervised learning — clustering the listings
Reinforcement learning — rewarding the model per sale
Generative AI — writing listing descriptions
scenarios.why: The data is labeled (each row has the known sale price), and the goal is predicting a numeric value — textbook supervised learning, specifically regression. Unsupervised learning finds structure in unlabeled data; reinforcement learning learns from rewards over time.
scenarios.hint: Each training example already includes the right answer. What do we call learning from labeled examples?

scenarios.title: Spam or not spam
scenarios.situation: An email filter must decide 'spam' or 'not spam' for each incoming message, trained on a million previously labeled emails.
scenarios.prompt: What kind of ML task is this?
choices: Classification — predicting a category label
Regression — predicting a continuous number
Clustering — grouping unlabeled emails
Forecasting — predicting next quarter's spam volume
scenarios.why: Classification assigns each input to a discrete category (spam vs not spam) using labeled training data. Regression would predict a number like a price; clustering works without labels.
scenarios.hint: Is the output a number or a category?

scenarios.title: Reading the invoices
scenarios.situation: A company wants software to extract totals and dates from scanned PDF invoices, and to flag angry sentiment in support emails.
scenarios.prompt: Which AI workload categories are these?
choices: Computer vision for the scans, natural language processing for the emails
Both are natural language processing
Both are anomaly detection
Speech recognition for the scans, knowledge mining for the emails
scenarios.why: Extracting data from images/scans is computer vision (Document Intelligence is the Azure service family); analyzing sentiment in text is natural language processing. Matching the workload to the right category is the first step in choosing a service.
scenarios.hint: One input is pictures of text, the other is text itself. Which AI sense handles each?

scenarios.title: The biased hiring model
scenarios.situation: A resume-screening model trained on ten years of historical hires starts rejecting qualified candidates from certain universities at a far higher rate.
scenarios.prompt: Which responsible AI principle is primarily at stake?
choices: Fairness — AI systems should treat all groups equitably and avoid bias
Reliability — the model must return answers quickly
Inclusiveness — the user interface must support screen readers
Transparency — the model's weights must be published publicly
scenarios.why: Fairness means AI systems should not produce biased or discriminatory outcomes; training on historically biased data is the classic way bias creeps in. Microsoft's responsible AI principles also include reliability and safety, privacy and security, inclusiveness, transparency, and accountability.
scenarios.hint: The harm is unequal treatment of groups of people. Which principle names that harm?

scenarios.title: The chatbot draft
scenarios.situation: A support team wants a bot that drafts original replies to customer questions in natural language, not just picking from a FAQ list.
scenarios.prompt: What distinguishes this generative AI approach from a traditional chatbot?
choices: It creates new text token-by-token based on patterns learned during training
It searches the FAQ faster using an index
It translates the FAQ into more languages
It stores more FAQ entries in memory
scenarios.why: Generative AI models (like large language models) produce novel text, images, or code rather than retrieving canned responses. They predict likely continuations based on training patterns — powerful, but also why outputs must be verified for accuracy.
scenarios.hint: Retrieval picks an existing answer; generation does what instead?

scenarios.title: Orders and customers
scenarios.situation: A retailer stores customers and orders in tables with defined schemas, joining them on customer IDs for reports.
choices: Structured schema with tables, rows, keys, and SQL querying
Schema-less JSON documents with flexible fields
Graph traversal for relationship queries
Time-series buckets for sensor data
scenarios.why: Relational databases organize data into tables with fixed schemas, enforce relationships via keys, and query with SQL — ideal for transactional data like orders and customers where structure is stable and integrity matters.
scenarios.hint: Tables, rows, keys, joins, SQL — what database family is that?

scenarios.title: The product catalog
scenarios.situation: A catalog stores products where each item has wildly different attributes — books have page counts, TVs have screen sizes — and the schema changes weekly.
choices: A NoSQL document store like Azure Cosmos DB
A relational database with a fixed schema
A data warehouse with nightly batch loads
A file share with CSV exports
scenarios.why: Document databases store flexible, schema-less JSON-like documents, so each product can carry different attributes without migrations. Relational schemas would need constant ALTER TABLE churn for this shape of data.
scenarios.hint: The attributes differ per item and change often. Which store embraces flexible schemas?

scenarios.title: Checkout vs quarterly report
scenarios.situation: The checkout system processes thousands of small transactions per second; the finance team runs heavy aggregations over five years of sales once a quarter.
choices: Checkout is OLTP (many fast transactions); the report is OLAP (complex analytics over large history)
Both are OLTP workloads
Checkout is OLAP; the report is OLTP
Both are streaming workloads
scenarios.why: OLTP systems handle many small, fast read/write transactions (checkout); OLAP systems run complex analytical queries over large historical datasets (quarterly reporting). They are optimized so differently that they usually live on different platforms.
scenarios.hint: Fast small writes versus big slow reads — which acronym matches each?

scenarios.title: Fraud in real time
scenarios.situation: A bank scores transactions for fraud. One team analyzes yesterday's full transaction log each morning; another needs a decision within seconds of each swipe.
choices: Batch processing for the morning analysis; stream processing for the per-swipe scoring
Stream processing for both
Batch processing for both
Neither — both are OLTP
scenarios.why: Batch processing handles large volumes on a schedule (the morning job); stream processing handles data continuously with low latency (per-swipe fraud scoring). The latency requirement is what forces the choice.
scenarios.hint: Seconds of latency versus a morning schedule — which model serves each?

scenarios.title: Raw and refined
scenarios.situation: A data team lands raw CSVs, images, and JSON in cheap storage, then curates clean tables for analysts to query with SQL.
choices: A data lake for raw storage feeding a data warehouse for curated analytics
Two data warehouses replicating each other
A transactional database with read replicas
A data lake used directly by BI tools with no curation
scenarios.why: A data lake stores raw data in any format cheaply at scale; a data warehouse stores curated, structured data optimized for SQL analytics. The lake-to-warehouse flow (often called ELT) is the standard modern pattern.
scenarios.hint: Where does raw data land cheaply, and where do analysts run clean SQL?

scenarios.title: Transform before or after
scenarios.situation: An engineer debates whether to clean and reshape data before loading it into the analytics platform, or load it raw and transform it there.
choices: ETL transforms before loading (good for strict schemas); ELT loads raw first and transforms in-platform (good for scale and flexibility)
ETL is always faster than ELT
ELT only works with relational sources
They are identical; the letters are just marketing
scenarios.why: ETL (extract, transform, load) cleans data before it lands — classic for warehouses with rigid schemas. ELT (extract, load, transform) lands raw data first and transforms inside the platform's compute — the modern cloud pattern that scales with cheap storage and elastic compute.
scenarios.hint: Does the cleaning happen before the data arrives, or after it's already inside?

scenarios.title: Never trust, always verify
scenarios.situation: A company historically trusted everything inside its corporate network. After a breach that started from a compromised internal laptop, leadership wants a new model.
scenarios.prompt: What is the core Zero Trust principle?
choices: Verify explicitly — authenticate and authorize every access request regardless of network location
Trust any device on the corporate VPN
Remove all firewalls since the perimeter failed
Require VPN for remote users only
scenarios.why: Zero Trust assumes breach and verifies each request explicitly based on identity, device health, and context — 'never trust, always verify.' The old castle-and-moat model trusted the internal network, which is exactly what the attacker exploited.
scenarios.hint: If the attacker is already inside, what must you still check on every request?

scenarios.title: Layers of the onion
scenarios.situation: A security architect proposes identity controls, network segmentation, encrypted storage, and application firewalls — saying no single layer should be the only protection.
choices: Defense in depth — layered controls so one failure doesn't mean compromise
Zero Trust — which forbids layered controls
The shared responsibility model — which is only about billing
Least privilege — which applies only to passwords
scenarios.why: Defense in depth layers security controls (physical, identity, perimeter, network, compute, application, data) so that if one layer fails, others still protect the asset. It complements Zero Trust rather than replacing it.
scenarios.hint: No single layer is trusted alone — what is layering called?

scenarios.title: Who patches the OS?
scenarios.situation: A team moves from VMs to Azure SQL Database and argues about who is responsible for patching the underlying operating system.
scenarios.prompt: How does the shared responsibility model answer this?
choices: Responsibility shifts with the service model — on PaaS like SQL Database, Microsoft manages the OS; on IaaS VMs, the customer patches the guest OS
Microsoft patches everything in all models
The customer patches everything in all models
Patching responsibility is decided per subscription by support ticket
scenarios.why: Shared responsibility: the more managed the service, the more Microsoft owns. IaaS (VMs) leaves the guest OS and apps to you; PaaS (SQL Database) moves the OS, patching, and high availability to Microsoft; you always own your data and identities.
scenarios.hint: Who owns the OS layer on a VM versus on a managed database service?

scenarios.title: Stolen drive scenario
scenarios.situation: A decommissioned disk from a datacenter ends up resold. The CISO asks whether customer data on Azure Storage could be read from it.
scenarios.prompt: What protects the data at rest?
choices: Storage Service Encryption encrypts data at rest by default with Microsoft-managed keys
TLS encrypts data at rest
RBAC encrypts data at rest
Resource locks encrypt data at rest
scenarios.why: Azure Storage encrypts all data at rest automatically using Storage Service Encryption (256-bit AES), so a stolen physical disk yields ciphertext. TLS protects data in transit; RBAC controls access but doesn't encrypt.
scenarios.hint: Which control scrambles the bits sitting on the disk itself?

scenarios.title: The traffic flood
scenarios.situation: A public-facing web app is hit by a volumetric attack saturating its network pipe. The team wants always-on network-layer protection tuned to the app's traffic.
choices: Azure DDoS Protection (Network Protection tier) on the virtual network
A network security group rule alone
Azure Firewall's FQDN filtering
Enabling a resource lock on the app
scenarios.why: Basic DDoS protection is automatic and always on; the Network Protection tier adds adaptive tuning, attack analytics, and cost protection for the VNet's public IPs. NSGs filter traffic but don't absorb volumetric floods.
scenarios.hint: You need to absorb a flood at the network layer, tuned per app. Which tier does that?

scenarios.title: The secure score
scenarios.situation: A CISO wants one dashboard showing misconfigurations across all Azure subscriptions plus prioritized remediation steps.
choices: Microsoft Defender for Cloud — CSPM with Secure Score and recommendations
Microsoft Sentinel — which is a SIEM, not a posture dashboard
Azure Policy — which enforces but doesn't score posture
Azure Monitor — which tracks performance metrics
scenarios.why: Defender for Cloud continuously assesses your cloud posture (CSPM), computes a Secure Score, and gives prioritized recommendations; its workload protections add threat defense. Sentinel is for security operations/SIEM on top of that data.
scenarios.hint: Posture assessment and a score across subscriptions — which service owns that?

scenarios.title: The steady workload
scenarios.situation: A company runs the same set of VMs 24/7 for a three-year application contract. They're paying full pay-as-you-go rates.
scenarios.prompt: What pricing option should they consider?
choices: Reserved capacity — commit to 1 or 3 years for a significant discount on steady workloads
Spot VMs — cheapest but evictable when Azure needs capacity
Pay-as-you-go — already optimal for steady workloads
Azure Hybrid Benefit — only for Linux VMs
scenarios.why: Reserved instances/capacity trade commitment (1 or 3 years) for deep discounts — ideal for predictable 24/7 workloads. Spot VMs are cheaper but can be evicted anytime, which suits interruptible batch jobs, not contracted steady workloads.
scenarios.hint: The usage is predictable for years. Which option rewards commitment?

scenarios.title: The render farm
scenarios.situation: A studio renders animation frames in parallel; if a node is reclaimed mid-job, the frame just re-queues with no business impact.
choices: Spot VMs — deep discounts for interruptible workloads that tolerate eviction
Reserved instances — for workloads that can't tolerate eviction
Dedicated hosts — for physical isolation
Pay-as-you-go — the only option for batch work
scenarios.why: Spot VMs use spare Azure capacity at steep discounts with the trade-off that they can be evicted with short notice. Re-queueable render frames are the textbook interruptible workload; anything needing guaranteed capacity should avoid spot.
scenarios.hint: The job survives losing a node. Which pricing exploits spare capacity?

scenarios.title: The migration business case
scenarios.situation: A CFO asks: 'What will it cost to run our datacenter workloads in Azure over three years, versus refreshing our hardware?'
choices: The Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) Calculator — compares on-premises costs to Azure
The Pricing Calculator — estimates a single bill, not a migration comparison
Azure Advisor — gives optimization recommendations, not migration TCO
Cost Management budgets — track spend after migration
scenarios.why: The TCO Calculator models your current on-premises costs (hardware, power, labor) against projected Azure costs for a migration business case. The Pricing Calculator estimates the cost of specific Azure services; Cost Management tracks actual spend afterward.
scenarios.hint: Which tool compares 'keep the datacenter' against 'move to Azure'?

scenarios.title: The surprise bill
scenarios.situation: A dev team left expensive VMs running over a long weekend and got a shocking invoice. They want an early warning next time.
choices: A Cost Management budget with alert thresholds on the subscription or resource group
An Azure Policy that deletes VMs on weekends
A resource lock on the subscription
A longer SLA on the VMs
scenarios.why: Cost Management budgets let you set spending thresholds with email alerts (e.g., at 80% and 100% of budget) so teams get warned before the invoice lands. Policies can enforce rules, but budgets-plus-alerts is the early-warning mechanism.
scenarios.hint: They want a warning before the money is spent. Which feature watches spend and emails?

scenarios.title: Chained dependencies
scenarios.situation: An app depends on two services, each with a 99.9% SLA. The architect claims the app therefore has a 99.9% SLA.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct composite SLA reasoning?
evidence: web tier → Service A (SLA 99.9%) → Service B (SLA 99.9%), all required per request
choices: Multiply them: 0.999 × 0.999 ≈ 99.8% — the chain is weaker than any single link
Take the higher of the two: 99.9%
SLAs don't combine; each stands alone
scenarios.why: Composite SLA for serial dependencies is the product of the individual SLAs: 99.9% × 99.9% ≈ 99.8%. Every dependency you add lowers overall availability — a key reason architects minimize critical-path dependencies and design for redundancy.
scenarios.hint: If either service failing breaks the app, is the app more or less reliable than each service?

scenarios.title: The idle VM
scenarios.situation: Azure Advisor flags a VM that has averaged 4% CPU for 30 days and recommends resizing or shutting it down.
choices: Cost optimization — identifying underutilized resources to reduce spend
Enforcing a security policy
Calculating the composite SLA
Applying a resource lock
scenarios.why: Azure Advisor's Cost recommendations surface underutilized resources (low-CPU VMs, unattached disks) to cut waste. Advisor also covers Security, Reliability, Operational Excellence, and Performance — but this recommendation is pure cost hygiene.
scenarios.hint: Low CPU for a month means paying for idle capacity. Which Advisor category is that?

scenarios.title: Fifty subscriptions
scenarios.situation: An enterprise has 50 subscriptions across business units and needs one place to apply a policy like 'no resources outside EU regions' to all of them.
choices: Management groups — a hierarchy above subscriptions where policy and RBAC assignments inherit downward
Putting all resources in one resource group
A single Azure Policy assigned per VM
Virtual network peering across subscriptions
scenarios.why: Management groups sit above subscriptions in the hierarchy (root → groups → subscriptions → resource groups). Policies and RBAC assigned at a management group inherit to everything below — the only sane way to govern at enterprise scale.
scenarios.hint: You need one assignment to cover fifty subscriptions. What sits above subscriptions?

scenarios.title: Who vs what
scenarios.situation: A junior admin confuses two assignments: one grants a user 'Contributor' on a resource group; another blocks VM SKUs larger than D-series across the subscription.
choices: The first is RBAC (who can do what); the second is Azure Policy (what rules resources must follow)
Both are RBAC assignments
Both are Azure Policy definitions
The first is a resource lock; the second is RBAC
scenarios.why: RBAC governs identity access (who can perform which actions). Azure Policy governs resource compliance (rules resources must satisfy, like allowed SKUs or regions). They answer different questions: access vs. compliance.
scenarios.hint: One answers 'can this person act?' and the other 'may this resource exist?' — which is which?

scenarios.title: The accidental deletion
scenarios.situation: A script with broad permissions deletes a production database during a cleanup run. The team wants a guardrail that blocks deletion regardless of permissions.
choices: A CanNotDelete resource lock on the production resources
An RBAC deny assignment on the script
A shorter backup retention policy
A policy that requires tags
scenarios.why: Resource locks (CanNotDelete, ReadOnly) block delete/modify operations even for users with permission — they're the guardrail against accidents and rogue automation. RBAC grants access; locks override it for protection.
scenarios.hint: You need something that says 'no' even to an admin with full rights. What does that?

scenarios.title: The mystery bill
scenarios.situation: Finance can't tell which department's resources generated each line of the Azure invoice.
choices: Consistent resource tagging (e.g., department, cost-center, environment) enforced by policy
Renaming all resources with department prefixes
Creating a separate tenant per department
Enabling diagnostic logs on every resource
scenarios.why: Tags are key-value metadata on resources that Cost Management can group and filter by — the standard mechanism for chargeback/showback. Enforcing required tags with Azure Policy keeps the data clean as teams deploy.
scenarios.hint: What metadata travels with each resource into the billing data?

scenarios.title: Finding the PII
scenarios.situation: A company doesn't know which of its thousands of data assets contain customer PII, and auditors are asking.
choices: Microsoft Purview — data discovery, classification, and governance across the estate
Microsoft Sentinel — a SIEM for security events
Azure Monitor — infrastructure metrics and logs
Defender for Cloud — workload protection
scenarios.why: Microsoft Purview scans and catalogs data assets, classifies sensitive data (like PII), and tracks lineage — the governance answer to 'where is our sensitive data?' Sentinel hunts threats; Purview governs data.
scenarios.hint: You need a map of data with sensitive-data labels, not security alerts. Which service?

scenarios.title: Repeatable landing zone
scenarios.situation: An enterprise wants every new subscription to arrive with the same policies, RBAC roles, and resource groups — deployed repeatably.
choices: Deployment stacks or IaC templates (ARM/Bicep/Terraform) applied per subscription
Azure Blueprints — still the current recommended approach
Manually configuring each subscription in the portal
Emailing a checklist to subscription owners
scenarios.why: Repeatable environment setup is done with infrastructure as code — ARM/Bicep/Terraform templates or deployment stacks that stamp out policies, roles, and resource groups identically. (Note: the older Blueprints service was deprecated, so IaC is the current path.)
scenarios.hint: How do you stamp out identical environments without clicking through the portal each time?
